idea: Train a domain classifier and keep only target-like docs, deduplicated. Steps: (1) Fit TfidfVectorizer(analyzer='char_wb', ngram_range=(1,4), max_features=200k, sublinear_tf=True) on the first 2000 chars of each doc; positives = the 200 target_sample docs, negatives = a seeded random sample of 3000 pool docs; fit LogisticRegression(class_weight='balanced', C=10). Score all pool docs; then do one self-training round: retrain with the top 15% scored pool docs as positives and the bottom 50% as negatives, rescore. (2) Remove exact and near duplicates (hash of whitespace-normalised, lowercased first 500 chars; keep the first occurrence). (3) Drop docs shorter than 200 chars. (4) Rank the remaining docs by score, and take docs with probability > 0.5 (WikiText-style: '= Title =' headers, ' @-@ ', spaced punctuation). Count tokens with tiktoken gpt2 (or estimate len/4 if time is tight). If the kept set has >= T tokens, keep the top-scored T tokens' worth; if fewer, return just that set (it will be cycled) but, if it is below 0.5 T, top up with the next-highest-scored docs until 0.5 T. (5) Shuffle the final list with a Random seeded from CURATE_SEED and return.
why: Roughly half the pool is spam, code, forum junk and duplicates, so spending the fixed 9.8M-token budget only on deduplicated WikiText-style articles matching the target should cut bpb far more than any ordering tweak.
outcome: dev 1.9467 against 1.9636 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea:
Add a word-order (fluency) filter to remove the word-shuffled WikiText docs that the char_wb classifier cannot detect (e.g. the pool docs '= 2015 Monaco Grand Prix =\nthe , , The of that Grand May One...' and '= Poole =\ntown of / on , coast the is in...'). Keep the current pipeline, then before ranking/cutting:

(1) Build a set B of lowercased whitespace-token bigrams from all 200 target_sample docs (full text).

(2) For every candidate doc, split the first ~6000 chars after the first line (skip the '= Title =' header) into whitespace tokens. Compute hit = fraction of adjacent token pairs found in B. Also compute hit separately on the first and second half of those tokens and take the minimum, to catch partially shuffled docs.

(3) Calibrate the threshold without labels: compute the same statistic leave-one-out style on the target docs (cheap approximation: build B from the 100 even-indexed target docs and score the 100 odd-indexed ones). Set thr = 0.6 * the 5th percentile of those held-out target hit rates. Drop any pool doc with min-half hit < thr. Shuffled text should score several times lower than fluent text, so the margin is wide.

(4) As a second guard, also drop docs where the rate of the function bigrams {'of the', 'in the', ', and', '. the', 'to the'} per token is < 0.25x the target median, for docs with at least 100 tokens.

Then proceed as now: p > 0.5, rank, cut to T tokens, 0.5 T top-up drawn only from docs that pass the filter, seeded shuffle. If the filter removes more than 70% of the p > 0.5 docs, treat it as miscalibrated and disable it.
why: The pool samples show WikiText-looking docs whose words are shuffled; a char-n-gram classifier scores them as target-like, so they are probably consuming a sizeable share of the training budget with text that teaches the wrong word order, and a bigram hit-rate check against the target sample should separate them cleanly.
outcome: dev 1.9172 against 1.9467 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea:
Extend the fluency filter from the first ~6000 chars to the whole document, scored in windows, so docs that are damaged only later on (shuffled, spam or foreign text after a clean head) are dropped. Keep everything else unchanged: dedup, classifier, the existing head filter, p > 0.5, cut at T, top-up, seeded shuffle.

Implementation:
(1) For each doc, tokenise the full text after the header line with lower().split(). Compute flags[i] = (tok[i], tok[i+1]) in B. Split the flags into consecutive windows of 300 pairs, merging a final window shorter than 150 pairs into the previous one. Compute the hit rate per window and the function-bigram rate per window (same 5 bigrams as now).
(2) Calibrate without labels, as now: build B_even from the even-indexed target docs and compute per-window hit rates over the full text of the odd-indexed targets. Set win_thr = 0.6 * the 2nd percentile of those window hit rates. Also compute for each held-out target doc its fraction of windows below win_thr, and call the maximum max_frac.
(3) Drop a pool doc if its fraction of windows with hit < win_thr exceeds max(0.10, 2 * max_frac), or if any run of 2 or more consecutive windows has hit < 0.5 * win_thr, or if any run of 3 or more consecutive windows has zero function bigrams. Docs with fewer than 150 pairs are judged by the existing head rule only.
(4) Apply this lazily inside passes(r), only to docs that already pass the existing head filter, in classifier-rank order so that only about T tokens' worth of docs are scanned. Keep the TIME_FILTER guard and the 70% miscalibration switch-off, now applied to the combined filter.
why: The classifier reads only the first 2000 chars and the fluency filter only the first 6000, so long WikiText-looking docs with shuffled or junk later sections may still be using up part of the T-token budget; this is untested, and the filter's first version gave the largest gain so far.
outcome: dev 1.9199 against 1.9172 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add content-level near-duplicate removal by paragraph containment; the current dedup only hashes the first 500 chars, so it misses copies with a changed title or head, partial copies and truncated copies. Keep everything else unchanged: head-hash dedup, classifier, fluency filter, p > 0.5, cut at T, 0.5 T top-up, seeded shuffle.

Implementation, inside the final ranking loop in classifier-score order (best first):
(1) For each doc that passes the fluency filter, split the full text on '\n'. Keep lines with at least 80 chars after whitespace-normalising and lowercasing. Hash each kept line (md5 of the normalised line, or Python hash of it) and weight it by its length in chars.
(2) Keep a global set `seen_par` of paragraph hashes from docs already accepted. Compute dup_frac = (chars of this doc's kept lines whose hash is in seen_par) / (chars of all its kept lines). Count repeats within the same doc as seen too (a line repeated inside one doc counts as duplicate from its 2nd occurrence).
(3) If the doc has at least 3 kept lines and dup_frac > 0.5, skip it; it is not selected and its hashes are not added. Otherwise accept it and add its hashes to seen_par.
(4) Token counting and the T / 0.5 T cut are applied only to accepted docs, so skipped duplicates are replaced by the next-best-scored docs.
(5) Safety: if this step would skip more than 40% of the p > 0.5 passing docs, disable it and fall back to the current behaviour. Respect the existing time guards: past TIME_FILTER, accept without checking.
why: The pool is known to contain duplicates and the head-hash only catches copies with identical openings, so removing content-level copies should replace wasted repeated tokens with fresh in-domain text within the fixed T budget.
outcome: dev 1.9201 against 1.9172 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add a self-calibrating "order gain" test to the fluency filter, to catch word-shuffled or partly shuffled WikiText docs that still pass the absolute bigram-hit threshold. Shuffled text made of frequent tokens can reach a hit rate near thr by chance. Keep everything else unchanged: dedup, classifier, existing hit and function-bigram rules, p > 0.5, cut at T, 0.5 T top-up, seeded shuffle.

Implementation, inside _fluency / passes:
(1) For the body tokens of a doc (raise FLU_CHARS to 12000), compute hit_real = fraction of adjacent token pairs in B, as now.
(2) Compute hit_perm = the same fraction after permuting the same token list with random.Random(seed).shuffle. Average over 2 permutations.
(3) gain = (hit_real + 0.01) / (hit_perm + 0.01). Fluent text should give a gain well above 1; shuffled text gives about 1 whatever its vocabulary.
(4) Compute the gain on the first and second half of the tokens separately, each half permuted within itself, and take the minimum. Do this only when a half has at least 100 pairs; otherwise use the whole-window gain.
(5) Calibrate without labels: build B_even from the even-indexed target docs, compute min-half gain on the odd-indexed targets, and let g5 be the 5th percentile. Set gain_thr = 1 + 0.5 * (g5 - 1).
(6) Drop a doc with at least 100 tokens if its min-half gain < gain_thr.
(7) Keep the existing safeguards: the 70% miscalibration switch-off, now applied to the combined filter, and the TIME_FILTER guard. Evaluate lazily in classifier-rank order as now.
why: The absolute hit threshold (0.6 x the 5th percentile) is probably loose enough for shuffled docs made of common tokens to slip through, whereas comparing each doc with its own permuted copy separates fluent from shuffled text regardless of vocabulary, so it should remove the remaining shuffled docs from the training set.
outcome: dev 1.8334 against 1.9172 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea:
Extend the order-gain test (not the hit-rate test from rejected experiment 3) from the first 12000 chars to the whole document, in windows, so docs with a clean head but a shuffled, spam or foreign tail are dropped. Keep everything else unchanged: dedup, classifier, existing head rules (hit, function bigrams, min-half gain), p > 0.5, cut at T, 0.5 T top-up, seeded shuffle.

Implementation:
(1) Only for docs that pass the existing head filter and are longer than the head window (more than FLU_CHARS + 1500 chars), tokenise the full text after the header line with lower().split(). Split the tokens into consecutive windows of 400, merging a final window shorter than 200 into the previous one.
(2) Per window, compute gain = (hit_real + 0.01) / (hit_perm + 0.01) with the existing _gain_of (B = all target bigrams, 2 seeded permutations within the window).
(3) Calibrate without labels, as now: build B_even from the even-indexed targets and compute window gains over the full text of the odd-indexed targets. Let w2 be the 2nd percentile of all held-out window gains, and win_thr = 1 + 0.5 * (w2 - 1); use the rule only if win_thr > 1. Also compute each held-out target's fraction of windows below win_thr, and call the maximum max_frac.
(4) Drop a pool doc if its fraction of windows with gain < win_thr exceeds max(0.15, 2 * max_frac), or if it has 2 or more consecutive windows below win_thr.
(5) Evaluate lazily inside passes(r) in classifier-rank order, so only about T tokens' worth of docs are scanned. Keep the TIME_FILTER guard (past it, accept unchecked) and the 70% miscalibration switch-off, applied to the combined filter.
why: The order-gain statistic gave by far the largest gain (1.9172 to 1.8334) but only inspects the first 12000 chars, so long articles damaged later on, which carry many tokens, may still get through; this is a bet that such tail-damaged docs exist in the pool, which the earlier hit-rate window test (experiment 3, neutral) was too weak to settle.
outcome: dev 1.8333 against 1.8334 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add a rare-word (character damage) test to the fluency filter, to drop target-style docs with character-level corruption (typos, deleted or garbled characters, foreign or junk spans). Such docs keep their word order, so they can pass the bigram-hit and order-gain tests. Keep everything else unchanged: dedup, classifier, hit / function-bigram / order-gain rules, p > 0.5, cut at T, 0.5 T top-up, seeded shuffle.

Implementation:
(1) After the classifier, take the candidate rows with score > 0.5 (if fewer than 50, the top 2000 by score) plus the 200 target docs. For each, take the body tokens exactly as now: _body(d).lower().split(), the 12000-char window after the header. Build a document-frequency Counter over each doc's set of tokens.
(2) A token is "rare" if it contains at least one alphabetic character and its DF is <= 2, i.e. it appears in this doc and at most one other. Pool docs and target docs are counted the same way, so the statistic is comparable.
(3) For each doc with at least 100 body tokens, compute rare_rate = rare tokens / tokens on the first and second half of the tokens separately and take the maximum. Use the whole window if a half has fewer than 100 tokens.
(4) Calibrate without labels on the 200 target docs with the same statistic: rare_thr = max(1.5 * the 98th percentile of target max-half rare_rate, the 98th percentile + 0.02).
(5) In passes(r), also fail a doc with at least 100 tokens whose max-half rare_rate > rare_thr.
(6) Keep the existing safeguards: the 70% miscalibration switch-off on the combined filter, and the TIME_FILTER guard. If building the DF table would start after about 125 s, skip this rule.
(7) Print, or keep in a comment or debug variable, the number of docs removed by this rule and the total selected tokens.
why: The pool sample shows character-level damage (e.g. "cookng", deleted spans) that the word-order tests cannot see, and corrupted words are almost unique across the pool, so a rare-token rate calibrated on the target sample should remove the remaining damaged in-domain docs.
outcome: dev 1.8281 against 1.8334 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Tighten the damage filters so partly damaged WikiText docs no longer pass, and re-add the rare-word rule from experiment 7 in a case-sensitive form. Keep everything else unchanged: dedup, classifier, p > 0.5, cut at T, 0.5 T top-up, seeded shuffle, TIME_FILTER guard, 70% miscalibration switch-off.

(A) Stricter order gain.
- Set GAIN_FACTOR to 0.85 (from 0.5), so gain_thr = 1 + 0.85 * (g5 - 1), with g5 still the 5th percentile of held-out target gains.
- Compute the gain on 4 consecutive quarters of the body tokens, each permuted within itself, and take the minimum. Use quarters when each has at least 100 pairs, else halves (as now), else the whole window.
- Calibrate with the same quarter/half/whole statistic on the odd-indexed targets, with B built from the even-indexed ones.

(B) Stricter hit rate.
- Set FLU_THR_FACTOR to 0.85 (from 0.6).
- Use the same quarter/half minimum for the hit rate, calibrated the same way.

(C) Case-sensitive rare-token rule.
- Take the candidate rows with score > 0.5 (if fewer than 50, the top 2000 by score) plus the 200 target docs.
- Tokenise each with _body(d).split(), without lower(), and build a document-frequency Counter over each doc's set of tokens.
- A token is rare if it contains a letter and its DF is <= 2.
- For docs with at least 100 tokens, rare_rate = rare tokens / tokens, taken as the maximum over the first and second half (whole window if a half has fewer than 100 tokens).
- rare_thr = max(1.3 * the 97th percentile of the target rare_rate, that percentile + 0.015). Fail docs above rare_thr.
- Also compute up_rate = the fraction of alphabetic tokens that start with an uppercase letter. Fail docs with at least 100 tokens whose up_rate is below 0.5 * the 2nd percentile of the target up_rate, or above 2 * the 98th percentile. This catches docs that were entirely lowercased or uppercased.
- Skip (C) if it would start after about 125 s.

(D) Diagnostics: store in a module-level debug dict the number of docs failed by each rule, the number of p > 0.5 docs, and the total selected tokens.
why: The order-gain rule gave by far the biggest gain (1.9172 to 1.8334) and the rare-word rule also lowered bpb (1.8281), so damaged target-style docs are probably still getting through the loose thresholds and the case-insensitive checks, and stricter self-calibrated tests should remove more of them at the cost of only a few clean docs.
outcome: dev 1.8390 against 1.8334 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add three whole-document, target-calibrated "residual damage" rules, applied in the final ranking loop to docs that already pass the existing filter. Keep everything else unchanged: dedup, classifier, hit / function-bigram / order-gain rules and their constants, p > 0.5, cut at T, 0.5 T top-up, seeded shuffle. Rejected docs are simply skipped, so the next-best-scored docs replace them.

(A) Tokens-per-char rule (character damage, garbled or foreign spans, anywhere in the doc).
- In the chunked loop, split each doc's full text into two halves by characters and tokenise both with enc.encode_ordinary_batch. The doc's token count is the sum of the two, so there is no extra tokenising pass.
- tpc = max(tokens/chars of half 1, tokens/chars of half 2). Use the whole doc if it is shorter than 2000 chars.
- Calibrate on the 200 target docs with the same statistic: tpc_thr = max(1.08 * the 98th percentile, the 98th percentile + 0.015).
- Skip docs with tpc > tpc_thr.
- Disable this rule if tiktoken is unavailable or the time is past TIME_TOKENISE.

(B) Intra-document repetition rule.
- Split the full text on '\n', whitespace-normalise each line, and keep lines of at least 30 chars.
- rep_frac = chars in the 2nd and later occurrences of an identical line within the doc / chars of all kept lines.
- Skip docs with rep_frac > max(0.10, 3 * the maximum rep_frac over the target docs).

(C) Cross-document boilerplate rule.
- Before the loop, over the candidate rows with score > 0.5, count for each normalised line of at least 30 chars the number of distinct docs that contain it (Counter of line hashes).
- A line is boilerplate if it occurs in at least 5 distinct docs.
- bp_frac = chars in boilerplate lines / chars of all kept lines.
- Skip docs with bp_frac > 0.05.
- Skip this rule if it would start after about 120 s.

Safeguards.
- If (A), (B) and (C) together would skip more than 25% of the p > 0.5 docs that passed the existing filter, disable all three.
- Past the existing time guards, accept docs unchecked.
- Record the per-rule removal counts and the total selected tokens in a module-level debug dict.
why: Tightening the head-window thresholds hurt in experiment 8 while the rare-word rule in experiment 7 scored slightly lower bpb, which suggests some target-style docs still carry character damage or repeated and injected lines that the head-only word-order tests cannot see; these three rules target exactly that without touching clean docs.
outcome: dev 1.8355 against 1.8334 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add a self-checking second-stage "topic within the domain" selection. The stage-1 classifier, after self-training, only separates WikiText-style text from non-WikiText, so it cannot tell whether the target is a narrower subset of WikiText (both shown target docs are places: Mamilla, Reading). Keep everything else unchanged: dedup, stage-1 classifier, fluency / function-bigram / order-gain filter, seeded shuffle.

Implementation, after the fluency filter has been evaluated:
(1) Let P = candidate rows with stage-1 score > 0.5 that pass the filter. Skip the whole stage if len(P) < 500 or the elapsed time is over about 130 s.
(2) Vectorise the first 6000 chars of each P doc and of the 200 target docs with TfidfVectorizer(analyzer='word', lowercase=True, sublinear_tf=True, min_df=2, max_features=100000, dtype=float32).
(3) Run a 5-fold stratified cross-validation, with folds seeded from CURATE_SEED: LogisticRegression(class_weight='balanced', C=1, max_iter=200), positives = target docs, negatives = P docs. Collect out-of-fold decision scores for every target doc and every P doc. Compute the out-of-fold AUC of target vs P.
(4) If AUC < 0.70, the target is not distinguishable from the clean pool WikiText, so make no change and use the current selection.
(5) If AUC >= 0.70, the target is a subset. Set thr = the 10th percentile of the out-of-fold target scores. Rank P by out-of-fold stage-2 score, descending. Select the P docs with score >= thr, capped at T tokens. If that gives fewer than 0.35 T tokens, keep adding the next P docs in stage-2 order until 0.35 T. Never add docs outside P. Then apply the seeded shuffle.
(6) Record in a module-level debug dict the AUC, len(P), the tokens in P, and the tokens finally selected.
why: Whole-document damage rules (experiments 3, 6, 9) no longer move the score, so the remaining lever is matching the target's distribution inside clean WikiText; a cross-validated AUC gate makes this a no-op if the target is not a distinguishable subset, though I have only two target docs as evidence that it is.
outcome: dev 1.8332 against 1.8334 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add a whole-document, windowed rare-token (character damage) rule. Experiment 7 applied this idea to the first 12000 chars only, with a loose threshold, and scored 1.8281; this version covers the full text and is slightly tighter. Keep everything else unchanged: dedup, classifier, hit / function-bigram / order-gain rules and their constants, p > 0.5, cut at T, 0.5 T top-up, seeded shuffle.

Implementation:
(1) After the existing filter has been evaluated, let P = candidate rows with score > 0.5 that pass it (if fewer than 50, the top 2000 by score). For each P doc and each of the 200 target docs, tokenise the FULL text after the header line with lower().split(). Build a document-frequency Counter over each doc's set of tokens, pool and target counted the same way.
(2) A token is rare if it contains at least one alphabetic character and its DF is <= 2.
(3) Split each doc's tokens into consecutive windows of 300, merging a final window shorter than 150 into the previous one. Docs with fewer than 100 tokens are not judged. Per doc compute:
  - doc_rate = rare tokens / tokens over the whole doc
  - win_max = the maximum window rare rate
(4) Calibrate on the 200 target docs with the same statistics:
  - doc_thr = max(1.4 * the 97th percentile of target doc_rate, that percentile + 0.015)
  - win_thr = max(1.5 * the 99th percentile of all target window rates, that percentile + 0.03)
(5) Fail a P doc if doc_rate > doc_thr, or if at least 2 of its windows exceed win_thr, or if more than 15% of its windows exceed win_thr. Set status[r] = 0 for failed docs so the ranking loop skips them. Do not replace them with docs of score <= 0.5, except through the existing 0.5 T top-up.
(6) Safeguards: skip the rule if it would start after about 120 s. Disable it if it would fail more than 20% of P.
(7) Record in a module-level debug dict the number of docs failed by this rule, len(P), and the total selected tokens.
why: The rare-token rule is the only untried-in-full direction with a measured gain (1.8281 against 1.8334 in experiment 7), and extending it to the whole document with a modestly tighter calibrated threshold should remove more character-damaged target-style docs without the over-strict order-gain and hit changes that hurt experiment 8.
outcome: dev 1.8258 against 1.8334 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add a typo-specific character-damage rule: count rare tokens that are one edit away from a common token. This is a sharper version of the rare-token rules of experiments 7 and 11 (which scored 1.8281 and 1.8258), because legitimate rare names are seldom one edit from a common word, so the threshold can be much tighter. Keep everything else unchanged: dedup, classifier, hit / function-bigram / order-gain rules and constants, p > 0.5, cut at T, 0.5 T top-up, seeded shuffle.

Implementation, after the existing filter has been evaluated:
(1) Let P = candidate rows with score > 0.5 that pass the filter (if fewer than 50, the top 2000 by score). Tokenise the full text after the header line of each P doc and each of the 200 target docs with split(), case-sensitive. Build a document-frequency Counter over each doc's set of tokens, pool and target counted the same way.
(2) Define the vocabularies over purely alphabetic tokens of length >= 4:
  - COMMON = tokens with DF >= 10
  - RARE = tokens with DF <= 2
(3) Build a deletion index D (SymSpell style): D = COMMON plus every string obtained by deleting one character from a COMMON token.
(4) A RARE token w is typo-like if w is in D (it is a common word with one character deleted), or if any one-character deletion of w is in D (covers insertion, substitution and transposition). Compute this once per distinct rare token and cache the result in a dict.
(5) Per doc with at least 100 tokens, compute:
  - typo_rate = typo-like tokens / tokens over the whole doc
  - win_max = the maximum typo rate over consecutive 300-token windows, merging a final window shorter than 150 into the previous one
(6) Calibrate on the 200 target docs with the same statistics:
  - doc_thr = max(2 * the 98th percentile of target typo_rate, that percentile + 0.003)
  - win_thr = max(2 * the 99th percentile of all target window rates, that percentile + 0.01)
(7) Fail a P doc if typo_rate > doc_thr, or if at least 2 of its windows exceed win_thr. Set status[r] = 0 so the ranking loop skips it. Failed docs are replaced only through the existing rules, never by docs with score <= 0.5 except via the 0.5 T top-up.
(8) Safeguards: skip the rule if it would start after about 115 s, and stop judging (accept unchecked) past TIME_FILTER. Disable the rule if it would fail more than 30% of P.
(9) Record in a module-level debug dict the number of docs failed, len(P), and the total selected tokens.
why: The pool still contains WikiText docs with character-level typos (e.g. "adut", "Hey Good Looki '") that pass every word-order test, and the two generic rare-token rules already lowered dev bpb, so a more precise edit-distance typo detector should remove more of them while dropping fewer clean docs.
outcome: dev 1.8331 against 1.8334 for the best at the time, rejected
